title: Millikan's Oil Drop, Electron Beam Motion & Thomson's Experiment — 40 MCQs
description: Conceptual and numerical questions covering Millikan's oil drop experiment, motion of electron beams in electric and magnetic fields, and Thomson's experiment for specific charge.

questions.q: What is the primary objective of Millikan's oil drop experiment?
options: To measure the mass of an electron
To measure the charge of an electron
To measure the specific charge of an electron
To measure the radius of an electron
questions.explanation: Millikan's oil drop experiment was designed to measure the elementary electric charge (e) of an electron by balancing gravitational and electric forces on charged oil droplets.

questions.q: In Millikan's experiment, an oil drop is stationary when which of the following conditions is met?
questions.explanation: When the drop is stationary, the net force is zero. The downward weight is balanced by the sum of the upward upward buoyant (upthrust) force and the upward electric force.

questions.q: Which law is used to calculate the viscous force on the oil drop in Millikan's experiment?
questions.explanation: Stokes' Law (F = 6πηrv) is used to determine the viscous drag force acting on the oil drop as it falls through the air at terminal velocity.

questions.q: When an electron beam passes through a uniform electric field, the electrons are deflected in which direction relative to the field?
options: Along a parabolic path parallel to the field
questions.explanation: Because electrons carry a negative charge, the electric force on them is F = -eE, meaning they accelerate in the direction opposite to the electric field vector.

questions.q: The magnetic force on a charge q moving with velocity v at an angle θ to a magnetic field B is given by:
questions.explanation: The magnitude of the magnetic force is given by F = qvB sinθ, where θ is the angle between the velocity vector and the magnetic field vector.

questions.q: Thomson's experiment is primarily used to determine which of the following quantities for an electron?
questions.explanation: J.J. Thomson's experiment uses crossed electric and magnetic fields to determine the specific charge (the charge-to-mass ratio, e/m) of an electron.

questions.q: In a velocity selector, an electron beam passes undeflected when which of the following conditions is met?
options: Electric force is greater than magnetic force
Magnetic force is greater than electric force
Electric force is equal to magnetic force
questions.explanation: For the beam to pass undeflected, the net force must be zero. This occurs when the electric force (eE) exactly balances the magnetic force (evB).

questions.q: What is the SI unit of specific charge (e/m)?
questions.explanation: Specific charge is the ratio of charge (in Coulombs) to mass (in kilograms), so its SI unit is Coulombs per kilogram (C/kg).

questions.q: Cathode rays are essentially a stream of which particles?
questions.explanation: Cathode rays are streams of electrons emitted from the cathode of a discharge tube and accelerated toward the anode.

questions.q: If a charged particle moves parallel to a uniform magnetic field, the magnetic force acting on it is:
questions.explanation: Since the angle θ between velocity and the magnetic field is 0°, the magnetic force F = qvB sin(0°) = 0. No deflection occurs.

questions.q: In Millikan's experiment, if the radius of the drop is r, density of oil is ρ, and density of air is σ, what is the apparent weight of the drop?
questions.explanation: The apparent weight is the actual weight minus the buoyant force (upthrust). Volume is (4/3)πr³, so Apparent Weight = Volume × (ρ - σ) × g = (4/3)πr³(ρ-σ)g.

questions.q: An oil drop of mass 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg is balanced in a uniform electric field of 2000 V/m. What is the charge on the drop? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: For a stationary drop, qE = mg. So, q = mg/E = (1.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg × 10 m/s²) / 2000 V/m = 5 × 10⁻¹⁸ C.

questions.q: An electron is moving at 4 × 10⁷ m/s perpendicular to a magnetic field of 0.5 T. What is the radius of its circular path? (e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C/kg)
In Thomson's experiment, if the electric field is E and the magnetic field is B, the velocity of the undeflected electron beam is given by:
questions.explanation: For an undeflected beam, eE = evB. Solving for velocity gives v = E/B.

questions.q: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 100 V. What is its final velocity? (e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C/kg)
questions.explanation: From energy conservation, ½mv² = eV. Thus v = √(2(e/m)V) = √(2 × 1.76 × 10¹¹ × 100) = √(3.52 × 10¹³) ≈ 5.93 × 10⁶ m/s.

questions.q: When an electron beam passes through a uniform electric field, the path of the electron is:
questions.explanation: The electric field exerts a constant force on the electron perpendicular to its initial velocity. This produces a constant vertical acceleration, resulting in a parabolic trajectory.

questions.q: In Millikan's experiment, the terminal velocity of the freely falling drop is proportional to which power of its radius r?
questions.explanation: Terminal velocity v = 2r²(ρ-σ)g / 9η. Assuming density and viscosity are constant, v is directly proportional to r².

questions.q: If an electron enters a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to its direction of motion, its kinetic energy:
questions.explanation: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, doing no work on the electron. Thus, kinetic energy and speed remain constant.

questions.q: An electron moves in a magnetic field of 0.1 T in a circle of radius 1 mm. What is its speed? (e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C/kg)
In a velocity selector, if E = 2.0 × 10⁴ V/m and B = 0.5 T, the velocity of the undeflected electron is:
If the electric field in a Millikan setup is doubled, what happens to the charge required to balance a drop of constant mass?
questions.explanation: For balance, qE = mg. If E is doubled, q must be halved to maintain the same mg.

questions.q: An electron with charge -e and mass m enters a uniform electric field E. The magnitude of its acceleration is:
questions.explanation: Force F = eE. By Newton's second law, magnitude of acceleration a = F/m = eE/m.

questions.q: If the radius of an oil drop in Millikan's experiment is halved, its terminal velocity becomes (assuming other factors constant):
questions.explanation: Since terminal velocity v ∝ r², if r becomes r/2, the new velocity v' ∝ (r/2)² = r²/4. The terminal velocity becomes one-fourth (a quarter) of the original.

questions.q: An electron beam is deflected by an electric field E. If the accelerating voltage is V, the vertical deflection y is proportional to:
questions.explanation: The deflection y = (eEL²)/(2mv²). Since v² = 2eV/m, we get y = (eEL²)/(4eV) = EL²/4V. Hence, y is directly proportional to E/V.

questions.q: If a proton and an electron enter the same magnetic field with the same velocity perpendicular to the field, the ratio of the radii of their circular paths (r_proton / r_electron) is approximately:
questions.explanation: The radius r = mv / (eB). The magnetic field and velocity are the same. The charge magnitude is the same. Thus r ∝ m. Since a proton is about 1836 times heavier than an electron, r_proton / r_electron ≈ 1836.

questions.q: In Millikan's experiment, an oil drop of density 900 kg/m³ falls with a terminal velocity of 0.01 m/s in air (η = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ Pa·s). If air density is negligible, what is the radius of the drop? (g = 10 m/s²)

In Thomson's experiment, an electric field of 1.5 × 10⁴ V/m is applied between plates 0.05 m long. An electron accelerated by 600 V passes through it. What is the vertical deflection? (e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C/kg)
An electron is moving perpendicular to a magnetic field of 0.2 T. The frequency of its revolution is approximately: (e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C/kg)

In a Millikan oil drop experiment, a drop of mass 9.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg is suspended between two plates 0.5 cm apart. If the potential difference applied is 3000 V, what is the charge on the drop? (g = 10 m/s²)

An electron beam is accelerated from rest through a potential difference V and then enters a uniform magnetic field B perpendicular to its velocity. The radius of the circular path is r. What is the relation between r and V?
questions.explanation: r = mv / eB. Since v = √(2eV/m), substituting gives r = (m/eB)√(2eV/m) = √(2mV/e) / B. Therefore, r is proportional to the square root of V (√V).

questions.q: A proton and an alpha particle enter a uniform magnetic field perpendicularly with the same kinetic energy. The ratio of the radii of their circular paths (r_p / r_α) is:
questions.explanation: r = √(2mK) / qB. For a proton (m, e): r_p = √(2mK) / eB. For an alpha (4m, 2e): r_α = √(2(4m)K) / 2eB = 2√(2mK) / 2eB = √(2mK) / eB. Thus, r_p / r_α = 1:1.

questions.q: In a Millikan oil drop experiment, a drop falls under gravity with a terminal velocity v. When an electric field is applied opposing gravity, it moves upwards with the same terminal velocity v. If the apparent weight is W and the electric force is F, what is the relation between them?
questions.explanation: Falling: W = 6πηrv. Rising: F - W = 6πηrv. Since velocities are equal, 6πηrv = W. Thus F - W = W => F = 2W.

questions.q: An electron enters a uniform electric field E perpendicular to its initial velocity v₀. After traveling a distance x in the field, it exits. What is the angle of deflection θ with the original direction?
questions.explanation: Time t = x / v₀. Vertical velocity v_y = at = (eE/m)(x/v₀). Deflection angle θ is given by tan(θ) = v_y / v_x = (eEx / mv₀²) / v₀. Wait, tan(θ) = (eEx/mv₀) / v₀ = eEx / mv₀². Thus θ = tan⁻¹(eEx/mv₀²).

questions.q: An oil drop of radius r and density ρ is suspended in a Millikan experiment where the electric field is E. Neglecting buoyancy, the charge on the drop is q. If the drop's radius doubles while maintaining the same charge, what must E become to keep it suspended?
questions.explanation: For balance, qE = (4/3)πr³ρg. If r doubles, the weight increases by a factor of 2³ = 8. To maintain balance, the electric force must also increase by 8. Since F = qE and q is constant, E must become 8E.

questions.q: Two electrons are moving in the same magnetic field B in circular paths of radii r₁ and r₂. What is the ratio of their kinetic energies (K₁ / K₂)?
questions.explanation: Radius r = mv / eB, so v = reB/m. Kinetic energy K = ½mv² = ½m(reB/m)² = (e²B²r²)/2m. Therefore, K ∝ r². The ratio K₁/K₂ = (r₁/r₂)².

questions.q: In a velocity selector, an electron beam is undeflected when E = 5 × 10⁴ V/m and B = 0.5 T. If the magnetic field is turned off, what is the acceleration of the electron? (e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C/kg)
questions.explanation: Acceleration a = eE / m = (e/m)E = (1.76 × 10¹¹ C/kg) × (5 × 10⁴ V/m) = 8.8 × 10¹⁵ m/s².

questions.q: An electron and a proton enter a uniform magnetic field perpendicularly with the same momentum. The ratio of the radii of their circular paths (r_electron / r_proton) is:
questions.explanation: The radius of the circular path is r = p / qB. Since both particles have the same momentum (p) and the same charge magnitude (e), their radii will be exactly the same. Thus, the ratio is 1.

questions.q: In Millikan's experiment, the distance between the plates is 5 mm. An oil drop of mass 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ kg is balanced by applying a voltage of 625 V. How many excess electrons are on the drop? (g = 10 m/s², e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
An electron in a magnetic field of 0.1 T describes a circular path of circumference 1.0 m. What is its speed? (e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C/kg)
questions.explanation: Circumference = 2πr = 1.0 => r = 1 / 2π. Speed v = r(e/m)B = (1 / 2π) × (1.76 × 10¹¹) × 0.1 ≈ 2.8 × 10⁹ m/s.

questions.q: A particle of charge q and mass m is accelerated from rest by a potential difference V and enters a uniform magnetic field B perpendicularly. The radius of the circular path is given by:
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy ½mv² = qV => v = √(2qV/m). Radius r = mv / qB = m√(2qV/m) / qB = √(2qVm) / (qB).
